summary: The Incident Object Description Exchange Format defines a data representation for security incident reports and indicators commonly exchanged by operational security teams. This proposed standard describes an updated information model for IODEF and a data model specified in XML.

eli5.summary: When security teams tell each other about a break-in or attack, it helps if everyone fills out the same report form. This is the newer version of that form.

questions: format for sharing security incident reports
what is the incident object description exchange format
what is the iodef restriction attribute
subtitle: A common XML format for security teams to share incident reports, response requests and threat indicators.

tldr.problem: Security incident response teams (CSIRTs) constantly ask each other for help, such as filtering attack traffic or taking down a botnet, but without a shared format every exchange needs manual reading and re-typing.
tldr.mechanism: IODEF v2 defines an information model and an XML schema for incident reports, indicators of malicious activity, requested actions and sharing metadata, with built-in ways to extend it and to mark how widely each piece may be shared.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track document that obsoletes RFC 5070 and RFC 6685, adds indicator support to the original incident-report format, and breaks backward compatibility with version 1 in a few places.

today: RFC 7970 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2016. It obsoletes RFC 5070 and RFC 6685, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Shared Incident Format
sections.content:
Organizations need help from other parties to stop malicious activity aimed at their networks. That might mean asking an ISP to filter attack traffic, contacting a remote site to take down a botnet, or sharing watch lists of known malicious indicators inside a consortium.

The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) is an XML representation of computer security information commonly exchanged between Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) and other operational security teams. It conveys four kinds of information: indicators that characterize a threat, incident reports that document attacks, response activity taken or that could be taken, and metadata so these can be exchanged among parties.

The structure allows machine-to-machine exchange, automated processing so that appropriate courses of action run faster, and an ecosystem of interoperable tools. The RFC is clear about its limits: sharing is not purely a technical problem, and procedural, cultural, legal and trust barriers are not addressed by IODEF itself.

The RFC calls IODEF a transport format. The data model may not be the best format for archiving or for in-memory processing.
sections.eli5: Imagine every school sending lost-and-found notes in its own style. Nobody could sort them quickly. IODEF is one standard note card that every security team can read and fill out.

sections.title: Data Types and the Extension Type
sections.content:
The model uses a small set of data types, each tied to an XML Schema type. Integers and real numbers must be encoded in base 10. Binary data comes in two flavors, base64 (BYTE) and hexadecimal (HEXBIN). Enumerated values (ENUM) are keywords from an ordered list.

Several types exist mainly for operations work. A PORTLIST is a comma-separated list of numbers and ranges, for example 2,5-15,30,32,40-50,55-60. A TIMEZONE is an offset from UTC. Date-times describe a single instant, and ranges are not supported.

For text that people read, the ML_STRING type carries an optional xml:lang attribute and a translation-id attribute. Several instances with the same translation-id and the same parent are translations of one another, so one document can hold the same text in many languages.

The EXTENSION type is the generic escape hatch for information IODEF does not otherwise represent. Its required dtype attribute names the kind of content (for example string, integer, url, csv, winreg or xml), and its meaning and formatid attributes describe the semantics.
sections.eli5: Every blank on the form has a type, like a box for a number, a box for a date or a box for words. Words can be written in several languages, and a special blank at the end lets you add anything the form forgot to ask.

sections.title: The Information Model: Documents and Incidents
sections.content:
The model is a tree of classes. The top class is IODEF-Document, whose required version attribute MUST be 2.00. It holds one or more Incident classes plus optional AdditionalData extensions.

An Incident carries summary information about the whole incident. Its required purpose attribute explains why the information is being sent: traceback, mitigation, reporting, watch or other. Its optional status shows where the incident is in a workflow: new, in-progress, forwarded, resolved or future.

Each incident must have an IncidentID (a tracking number made unique by combining the CSIRT's fully qualified domain name with the number), a GenerationTime and at least one Contact. Optional children cover times such as DetectTime, StartTime and EndTime, plus a Discovery (how it was found), Assessment (impact), Method (techniques used), History (a log of actions) and IndicatorData.

New in version 2, RelatedActivity links an incident to earlier ones and attributes it to a ThreatActor or Campaign. The Contact class treats people and organizations alike and can nest inside itself, so a child contact inherits details such as the organization from its parent.
sections.eli5: The whole report is like a folder. Inside is a page for each incident: who is in charge, when it happened, how it was found, who was hurt and what was done about it. Pages can have smaller pages stapled to them.

sections.title: Sharing Rules and Observable Tags
sections.content:
Two attributes recur throughout the model. The restriction attribute says how the sender expects the recipient to handle the information in a class and its children. The values are public, partner, need-to-know, private and default, plus the color-style synonyms white, green, amber and red.

The value is logically inherited by child classes, but a child can set its own value to relax or tighten the policy. The default is private, but only on the Incident class. The RFC stresses that this is a guideline only: there are no technical means to ensure the recipient follows it.

The observable-id attribute tags a piece of data in the document so that an indicator can refer to it later. Its value is a unique identifier within the document, and the ObservableReference class uses it.
sections.eli5: Each page can be stamped with a sharing rule, like "anyone can read this" or "keep this secret". The stamp is a polite request, not a lock, so the reader has to be trusted to follow it.

sections.title: Describing Events, Impact and Requested Actions
sections.content:
An incident is usually made of individual events. EventData holds the details of each one: times, contacts, how it was discovered, the Method used, supporting Record data such as logs, and a Flow that lists the System classes (hosts or networks) involved. If an EventData conflicts with the summary in the Incident class, the more specific EventData MUST supersede it.

EventData can nest within itself. The nesting depth groups related information so no explicit identifiers are needed. For example, two hosts with different impacts but the same contact are two inner EventData classes under an outer one that holds the shared Contact.

The Assessment class describes the repercussions for the victim through system, business, time and monetary impact classes, and a Confidence class. A System can be classed as source, target, intermediate, sensor or infrastructure, and its spoofed attribute signals whether that role may be a decoy.

The Expectation class tells the recipient what the sender wants done. Its action attribute offers values from nothing and investigate to block-host, rate-limit-network, honeypot and watch-and-report. If an EndTime is given and the recipient cannot finish before it, the recipient MUST NOT carry out the action.
sections.eli5: An incident is a story told in scenes. Each scene says which computers were involved, what damage was done, and what the sender would like you to do next, such as "please block this address" or "just keep an eye out".

sections.title: Indicators and Observables
sections.content:
Version 2 adds support for indicators: observable features that help detect malicious activity, along with metadata. An IndicatorData class holds one or more Indicator classes. Each has an IndicatorID (the CSIRT's name, a version and an identifier), an optional validity window from StartTime and EndTime, and a Confidence estimate.

Every indicator MUST have exactly one of Observable, IndicatorExpression, ObservableReference or IndicatorReference. An Observable holds exactly one thing, such as an Address, DomainData, EmailData, FileData, CertificateData or a BulkObservable. A bulk observable lists many values of one type, one per line, for example IP addresses, domain names, file hashes or file paths.

An IndicatorExpression combines children as a boolean expression using its operator attribute: not, and, or or xor. The default is and, and a nested expression acts like parentheses. Invalid algebraic expressions MUST NOT be specified.
sections.eli5: An indicator is a wanted poster for a bad thing: a suspicious web address, a risky file, a strange email. You can say "watch for this one AND that one" or "this one OR that one" to make the poster more exact.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
Every IODEF document MUST begin with an XML declaration that states the XML version and the character encoding. UTF-8 SHOULD be used unless UTF-16 is necessary, and other encodings SHOULD NOT be used. The namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-2.0, and each document MUST reference the schema using xsi:schemaLocation.

Documents MUST be well-formed XML, and recipients are RECOMMENDED to validate against the schema in the RFC. Schema validity alone is not enough: the prose of the RFC adds constraints, such as which child classes must be present, that cannot easily be written in the schema. Because the registered enumerated values will grow, implementations SHOULD periodically update their schema.

Internationalization is built in. Each document MUST state its language, normally with xml:lang on the top element, and free-form text can override it. Implementations SHOULD pick the translation relevant to the recipient. Standardized enumerated values let a team make rough sense of a report even when the free text is in an unfamiliar language.
sections.eli5: Every report must say what alphabet and language it uses and which version of the form it is. The receiver should also check the report against the form's rules, including the rules that are written only in words.

sections.title: Extending IODEF and the IANA Registries
sections.content:
IODEF supports two kinds of extension. New classes are added with the generic EXTENSION type. Adding attributes to existing classes is not supported. New values for enumerated attributes are added by privately or publicly extending the list.

For private extension, every extensible attribute foo has a companion ext-foo. The sender sets foo to ext-value and puts the new value in ext-foo, for example type='ext-value' ext-type='new-attack-type'. The ext- attribute MUST NOT be set unless the main attribute is ext-value.

For public extension, version 2 creates 34 IANA registries of enumerated values, managed by Expert Review. The document also registers the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-2.0 and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:iodef-2.0.

Extensions that embed XML MUST declare a separate namespace. Implementations MUST NOT download schemas at runtime unless the right precautions are taken, and recipients MUST be prepared for a schema reference that never resolves. To tell which private extension a document uses, IODEF-Document has the private-enum-name and private-enum-id attributes, and only one private extension can be identified in a given document.
sections.eli5: If the form has no box for what you need, you may write in a new box and label it, or ask the official keeper of the form to add it for everyone. Never fetch unknown instructions from the internet while reading a report.

sections.title: What Changed From Version 1
sections.content:
Version 2 evolves the model in RFC 5070, which was developed primarily for incident reports. The new version adds indicators and reflects the challenges CSIRTs face now. It tried to preserve backward compatibility but could not do so in every case.

The largest additions are the observable-id attribute and IndicatorData class, the ThreatActor and Campaign classes for attribution, the Discovery class, and new classes such as DomainData, EmailData, FileData, CertificateData, HashData and SignatureData.

Incompatible changes include the version value (now 2.00), xml:lang now used on all multilingual strings, Service@ip_protocol renamed ip-protocol, formatid renamed format-id, and removal of the Impact, Fax and Node/NodeName classes. ReportTime is no longer required, while GenerationTime now is.
sections.eli5: The new form keeps most of the old boxes and adds new ones for warning signs and for who is behind an attack. A few old boxes were renamed or removed, so old filled-in forms need a little fixing.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The data model does not itself create security or privacy problems, but the data it carries can be sensitive. The messaging protocol used to exchange documents MUST provide appropriate confidentiality, integrity and authenticity. The RFC points to the Real-time Inter-network Defense protocol (RFC 6545) and its HTTP/TLS transport binding (RFC 6546) as providing this.

Because implementations may act on a document, they must authenticate the sender and the receiver. A recipient is free to ignore or refine the sender's Confidence values, and ambiguous Confidence elements MUST be ignored. Some classes, such as Confidence@rating='low' and DefinedCOA, need out-of-band agreement on their meaning before operational use.

Documents can carry executable content, through EXTENSION classes, RecordPattern, email attachments and DetectionPattern, so implementations MUST handle them with care to prevent unintentional automated execution.

On privacy, the identifiers in IODEF could be linked to people or organizations, and repeated exchanges can allow correlation. Personal identifiers should be shared only when necessary, transport security MUST provide document-level confidentiality, and the restriction attribute is only a guideline that the recipient can ignore.
sections.eli5: A security report can hold secrets about people and computers, so it must travel in a locked, verified envelope. The receiver should also be careful, because a report could hide something harmful inside.

viz.caption: KEY CLASSES OF AN IODEF DOCUMENT (SIMPLIFIED FROM THE RFC FIGURES)

items.label: public (white)
items.desc: Can be freely distributed without restriction.

items.label: partner (green)
items.desc: May be shared within a closed community of peers, partners or affected parties, but not openly published.

items.label: need-to-know (amber)
items.desc: May be shared only within the organization with individuals who need to know.

items.label: private (red)
items.desc: May not be shared. The default on the Incident class.

items.label: default
items.desc: Shared according to a disclosure policy pre-arranged by the communicating parties.

items.label: nothing
items.desc: No action is requested. Do nothing with the information.

items.label: contact-source-site
items.desc: Contact the site(s) identified as the source of the activity.

items.label: investigate
items.desc: Investigate the system(s) listed in the event.

items.label: block-host
items.desc: Block traffic from the machine(s) listed as sources in the event.

items.label: rate-limit-network
items.desc: Rate-limit the traffic from the network(s) listed as sources in the event.

items.label: honeypot
items.desc: Redirect traffic from systems listed in the event to a honeypot for further analysis.

items.label: upgrade-software
items.desc: Upgrade or patch the software or firmware on an asset listed in the event.

items.label: watch-and-report
items.desc: Watch for the described activity or indicators, and notify the sender when seen.

items.label: defined-coa
items.desc: Perform a predefined course of action named in the DefinedCOA class.
